compression.title: Negotiating Tech
compression.lede: is the UC Berkeley Labor Center's searchable inventory of how U.S. unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining: over 950 contract provisions from more than 175 agreements (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).

sentences.text: Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is, in its own words, a searchable inventory that "documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining" (Labor Center page); the Labor Vector census files it as a searchable inventory whose evidence is the negotiated provision, at its intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record).

It is designed "to help users locate and understand how unions have addressed workplace technologies in collective bargaining agreements", "as an informational resource rather than a source of model language", highlighting "actual negotiated provisions" and the strategies unions have used in practice (Labor Center page); the census carries the limit as its first negative tag, "NOT model contract language" (Labor Vector record).

Its unit is the provision, "either direct excerpts of contract language or paraphrased summaries", each "accompanied by a link to the complete collective bargaining agreement", a clause touching several issues appearing in more than one subsection, and references to specific employers or unions "generally omitted" (Labor Center page); the census states the unit as "a technology-related provision of a U.S. collective bargaining agreement", linked to the full contract and coded (Labor Vector record).

The contracts came from the Department of Labor's OLMS repository, the Office of Personnel Management's CBA database, union and employer websites and direct contributions from unions; they were found by keyword searches "focused on terms such as surveillance, monitoring, and automation, followed by manual review", and each provision was coded on "four key dimensions: bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).

Over 500 agreements of public and private sector unions across a range of industries were reviewed, more than 175 with technology-related provisions were included, and over 950 provisions are referenced, from "contracts negotiated across several decades" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It is arranged in six sections: definitions of workplace technologies and of technological change itself, laid as "a foundation for worker protections, employer responsibilities, and union involvement"; foundational rights, "advance notice, information, negotiation, participation, and jurisdiction, typically outlined in technological change clauses"; employer commitments on "job security, pay, retraining, and safe, accessible working conditions"; the governance of workplace technology applications; joint committees and other mechanisms "for co-governance of workplace technologies"; and provisions on data collection, data rights, telework and remote work (Labor Center page).

Its fourth section holds provisions "that govern the use of workplace technologies, including electronic monitoring and surveillance, HR and workforce management systems, and job-related digital tools", with Section 4.4 a list of named technologies (Labor Center page); the census pairs it with the worked question "Where are actual negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline?", since "A protection is evidence when it is written into an agreement or a rule", its role there "U.S. union contract provisions on notice, information, monitoring, data rights and job security, each linked to its agreement" (Labor Vector worked questions).

Many provisions refer broadly to "technology" or "technological change", some to "automation", and such broad terms allow "a single clause to cover diverse technologies", which the page values for "preemptive language that secures rights and protections in anticipation of, or prior to, the adoption of new technologies" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).

Others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers, handheld devices or internet-based tools; "A few recent contracts explicitly reference artificial intelligence or generative AI, though most do not name AI or other emerging technologies directly", and specific language is "more common in clauses focused on the governance and regulation of how particular technologies are used in the workplace, often involving mechanisms for participatory oversight or joint decision-making" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).

Some contracts were established many years ago, "showing that longstanding language around technology remains relevant even as new innovations emerge" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).

The census reads it by its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains": the labor is that of "union-represented workers covered by the agreements", in public and private sectors where employers introduce or use workplace technologies; it is directed by employers, "with the union rights to notice, information, negotiation, participation and co-governance the provisions secure"; and gains are "not recorded as outcomes", the provisions recording negotiated guarantees around job security, pay, retraining and working conditions (Labor Vector record).

In the census's own reading, kept apart from the resource's terms, "The inventory records negotiated limits on how employers direct work through technology; it meets the directionality stack at the contract layer, where workers hold rights to notice, negotiation and joint oversight", and "It holds no measure of task fidelity or user labor drag" (Labor Vector record).

Its stated limits are the page's: "not exhaustive of all sectors"; many agreements "don’t mention specific technologies by name" and use functional terms like "automated", "electronic" or "monitoring", so that a search by technology misses them; and employer and union names are omitted (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, stated limits).

The census holds that it can answer "what U.S. unions have negotiated on technology: notice, information, participation, job security, pay, retraining, monitoring, data rights, telework" and "how contract language names or leaves unnamed specific technologies, AI included" (Labor Vector record).

It cannot answer "whether the provisions are enforced or what they change at work", "how common any provision is across all U.S. contracts", or "bargaining outside the United States", and the census tags it "NOT a census of all U.S. contracts", "NOT a measure of outcomes for workers" and "U.S. agreements only"; the worked question's gap is that "None of the three records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (Labor Vector record; worked questions).

The archive reads collective bargaining, the means the inventory's page names, as a class in U.S. law: "law is historically where labor's radical potential gets translated into managed rights", among them a right to bargain within the wage system, and "The National Labor Relations Act (1935) was explicitly designed to channel labor conflict into administrable forms", so that the law recognizes labor insofar as labor becomes governable (#239).
In #239's list of what law does to labor, "Collective bargaining" survives while "Class antagonism" is excised: "The law speaks labor's language while administering labor's containment" (#239).

#1439 names organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, its demands including "limits on surveillance and forced adoption", its instruments "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule", measured by union density and contract terms, a sense it states "is the majority usage, it is well founded, and the disputes it names are material"; and it records that the retrieval layer, queried, returns that sense almost exclusively (#1439).

#256 defines the archive's Assembly against the union: "Unions are legal entities with membership, dues, and collective bargaining rights. The Assembly is a structural position, not an institution" (#256).

It "was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge as a project of the UC Berkeley Labor Center’s Technology and Work Program", with Kresge its contact, is cited as Kresge, July 2025, Center for Labor Research and Education, University of California, Berkeley, and was funded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, operator, founded).

It was last updated on July 2, 2025, and its makers "plan to update this inventory periodically" and invite suggestions; each contract is labeled by the acronyms of its negotiating unions with an identifier of its source, OLMS, OPM or PCBA; the page carries "© Copyright 2026 UC Berkeley Labor Center", and the census records it as active, a public searchable website, with no open licence stated, read 2026-10-29 (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).

The census sets it beside Coworker's bossware database, whose "Little Tech report acknowledges Lisa Kresge", and the ILO platform policy tracker, whose "CBA component also holds collective agreements, for platform work in the European Union", and leaves unchecked the six section pages and their provisions, the linked contracts, and the count of provisions naming AI or generative AI (Labor Vector record, relations, unchecked).

Its short name, also given as "Negotiating tech", is also the name of a common question: "Two words that name an inventory of union contracts also name the commonest question a tech worker asks, and the Overview answers that question"; "The name is also salary negotiation, and the composition gives that sense" (Labor Vector record, aka; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

At "Negotiating Tech" on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the inventory's page was the first card, dated "Jul 2, 2025" and carrying the page's first sentence: "The retrieval held the target (it is card 1, with the inventory's own self-description and its 2 July 2025 date) and the composition did not use it"; no person, institution or identifier is in the answer, and thirteen cards of individual salary negotiation follow (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry reads a reversal: "The inventory records collective bargaining over technology at work; the composition gives individual bargaining for pay in the technology industry", "One question about worker power answered with its opposite unit of bargaining", bargaining composed "as an individual employee's tactics toward an employer" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It codes the answer generic and not substitute, "No entity stands in the target's place", and not an inversion, since "no element of the inventory is carried into the composition; the name is read as a phrase": the name token occurs only in card titles, and "the collective sense loses to the individual one, though the collective sense holds the first card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It holds that the record's full title, "An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age", "is the address that would reach it", and that the census record, which landed on laborvector.org the same day, is cited by no card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
